summary: Year 2 learners describe 2-D shapes by number of sides and by line symmetry (specifically a vertical line). The conceptual crux is that a line of symmetry is a FOLD line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (mirror images that coincide) — NOT merely a line that splits a shape into two same-sized pieces. The decisive non-example is the diagonal of a non-square rectangle: it makes two congruent triangles yet does not coincide on folding. Physical folding of paper cut-outs and mirrors let children verify matching rather than judging by eye; side-count combines with symmetry to tell shapes apart.
misconceptions: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking the halves coincide.
Thinks any line that cuts a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — e.g. accepts the diagonal of a rectangle because it makes two identical triangles.
Judges 'the halves are the same' by eye/size rather than by folding or mirroring to see if they actually land on each other.
Confuses the vertical line of symmetry with 'any line through the centre' and does not realise a shape can have several (or no) lines of symmetry.

activities.title: Fold test: does each half land on the other?
steps: Cut out a paper/card rectangle (a non-square one).
Fold it along the vertical line down the middle: check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Now fold the same rectangle corner-to-corner along the diagonal and watch what happens to the corners.
Say out loud for each fold whether it is a line of symmetry and why.
Repeat the fold test on other cut-out shapes (square, triangle), hunting for every fold where the halves coincide.
activities.insight: A line of symmetry is a fold where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (coincide), not just a line that makes two pieces the same size. The diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but a corner overhangs when folded — so congruence is not enough.

activities.title: Mirror check and completing the mirror half
steps: Place a small mirror (or Mira) upright along a candidate line on a shape and look at the reflection.
Check whether the reflection in the mirror continues the shape exactly — if it does, the line is a line of symmetry.
On dot-paper or a pegboard, draw/build half of a pattern, then draw or build the missing mirror half so the whole is symmetric.
Describe one half as the reflection of the other, not just 'the same size'.
activities.insight: One half of a symmetric shape is the mirror image (reflection) of the other; reflecting, like folding, tests whether the halves actually coincide.

activities.title: Count sides and combine with symmetry to tell shapes apart
steps: Count the sides of a given 2-D shape by touching and marking each side as you count.
Count the lines of symmetry of the same shape by folding or mirroring.
Place a square beside a non-square rectangle and compare both properties: '4 sides AND how many lines of symmetry?'
State how the square differs from the rectangle using BOTH the number of sides and the number of lines of symmetry.

Try the same shapes turned to different angles and fold or mirror-test again to confirm they still have the same lines of symmetry. The lines turn with the shape, so a line that was vertical may now be slanted or horizontal.
activities.insight: Shapes are described and distinguished by combining properties — a square and a non-square rectangle both have 4 sides, but a square has four lines of symmetry and this rectangle has two. Symmetry is a property of the shape, not of how it sits on the page.

activities.title: Predict-then-fold diagnostic conversation
steps: Before folding, predict: 'If we fold this non-square rectangle exactly along its diagonal, corner to corner, will the two halves land exactly on top of each other?' Say yes or no first.
Fold along the diagonal and compare what happened to your prediction.
Explain in your own words why two halves being the same size is not enough for a line of symmetry.
Show, by folding, which lines of a square are lines of symmetry and which lines of the rectangle are not.
activities.insight: Committing to a prediction before folding surfaces whether you are reasoning about matching halves or about equal-sized pieces; the overhang resolves it.

checkQuestion: Show the child a non-square rectangle with two lines drawn on it: one straight down the middle (vertical) and one from corner to corner (the diagonal). Ask: 'Which of these lines are lines of symmetry for the rectangle? How would you check?'
checkAnswer: The vertical line down the middle IS a line of symmetry — folding along it, the two halves land exactly on top of each other. The diagonal is NOT — folding along it, the two triangular halves do not coincide (a corner overhangs). The check is to fold (or use a mirror) and see whether the halves land on each other, not merely whether they are the same size.
